title: Live updates from the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Thailand as financial leaders take on AI, debt, and geopolitical upheaval
author: dhojnacki
text:
The world’s finance ministers and central bank governors are gathering in Bangkok, Thailand this week for the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank. Our experts are on the ground talking to leaders and getting the behind-the-scenes scoop on how the Bretton Woods institutions are taking on the most urgent challenges in the global economy, including conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, soaring public debt, and the impact of artificial intelligence (AI).

Check back for expert reactions to breaking news, updates from our events with high-level policymakers, and more.

OCTOBER 16 | 6:30 AM ET

“They finally get it.” Closing thoughts on Bangkok.

Josh Lipsky
Chair of international economics at the Atlantic Council; former IMF adviser

We’ve come to the end of another IMF-World Bank Week, but it’s an IMF-World Bank Week unlike any other in the history of these institutions. Now it’s easy to say, well, because we were in Thailand and Bangkok, things felt different. And there’s no doubt things certainly felt different in these meetings. But it wasn’t just the atmosphere, and it wasn’t just the location. Something has changed in the ministers and the central bank governors, in the meetings and the conversations. And all week I’ve been struggling to figure out what it is. And it’s only today when we hosted India’s finance minister and France’s finance minister that it finally clicked for me what’s going on.

For three years I’ve come at the end of these meetings and given these remarks and basically issued a call to action to the IMF and the World Bank membership to say: “Wake up to the era of geoeconomics we live in. Remember the founding of these institutions, that national security and finance are interconnected. You can’t operate your policy devoid of the realities of geopolitics.”

And for three years those ministers have come here and tried to avoid those tough questions, and I understand completely why. It is not their training, it is not their experience, it is not what they signed up to do. They are trying to foster growth for their economies. But they have realized through hard experience of the shocks we have all experienced over the past several years that they do not live in that world anymore. And what’s different about these meetings is they finally get it. Minister after minister came to this desk and right before we went on camera, they would turn to me and turn to my colleagues and say: “Ask me the tough question. Ask me about what happened in Saudi Arabia. Ask me about Iran and the war.”

It was the opposite of what had happened before, something completely different. They had finally absorbed the reality of what we are living in—this tectonic shift in how geopolitics and finance works. And I think it’s for the better. I think it will lead to better policy. I think it will make everything we do here more relevant and, most importantly, it will deliver better growth for the people around the world, because the policies that are implemented will reflect the realities in which they have to be delivered. That is what this is all about: the simple and fundamental realization that peace and prosperity have always been and will always be interconnected. It is not a new idea. It is an old idea. And these leaders forgot it. But I am so grateful to be here because they have rediscovered it. And if the Atlantic Council in any small shape or form through our work have helped them rediscover it, then I’m incredibly proud of that.

We will continue that mission in the days, weeks, and months ahead. That will be our commitment. We believe that these institutions are vital for economic prosperity, but equally important, they are vital for global peace. We will continue that work. And I want to thank the incredible team, my colleagues at the GeoEconomics Center, the Engagement Team at the Atlantic Council, our team working around the clock back in DC, our AV squad right behind me who have put on these fifty events over the last five days. It has been a nonstop effort to bring the meetings around the world. We hope you have enjoyed the programming. We won’t stop here at the Atlantic Council. You can bet we’ll see you back in Washington, DC.

OCTOBER 16 | 5:00 AM ET

A sharper fiscal message but little policy momentum

Martin Mühleisen
Nonresident senior fellow at the GeoEconomics Center; former IMF chief of staff and strategy director

The frenetic energy of the city of Bangkok stood in sharp contrast to the subdued mood of financial policymakers gathered here this week. The ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and the Gulf continued to weigh on delegates, and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s absence diminished the gathering’s political weight. While the IMF delivered a stark warning about government finances in the World Economic Outlook, the meetings produced little in the way of policy agreements to take on hot topics like AI risks or regional integration.

Still, there were positive developments to be found as I walked the hallways of the convention center this week.

For instance, the Sovereign Debt Roundtable noted that all past debt restructuring cases were close to being completed. As for ongoing program cases, Senegal could become a test case for faster implementation of the Common Framework, while Argentina probably received the least amount of public attention since it returned to the multilateral fold in 2016.

The Bangkok Blueprint for Fraud-Resilient Financial Services, developed by the IMF, World Bank, and Bank of Thailand, was a win for the Thai hosts. The playbook for national policymakers addresses the risks that financial fraud poses to households, businesses, and confidence in digital financial services.

Thailand was a worthy setting to illustrate the current dynamics of the global economy. Southeast Asian economies have benefited from the diversion of US-China trade and strong demand for AI-related inputs. The rise of digital payments was evident on every street corner.

And inside the hall, the promises and challenges of AI, crypto assets, and blockchain-based payment mechanisms were a constant topic. Central bank digital currencies also remained a subject of debate. The European Central Bank continues to advance preparations for a digital euro, as ECB President Christine Lagarde shared from our studio, but views still differ on the benefits of particular models and on how best to improve cross-border payments.

The rhetoric from policymakers on the main stage or passing through our studio suggests they understand the urgency of the world’s growing economic vulnerabilities. But they will return to their respective capitals without much to show for it this time.

OCTOBER 16 | 4:10 AM ET

How AI can take central banks from forecasting to “nowcasting”

Amin Mohseni-Cheraghlou
Macroeconomist with the GeoEconomics Center; former senior advisor to the executive director at the IMF and research economist at the World Bank

During a fireside conversation in Bangkok today with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said: “[AI] is going to fundamentally change the conduct of monetary policy.” One way this will play out is the development of “nowcasting” tools.

Central bankers have traditionally guided economies through the rearview mirror using monthly, quarterly, or annually collected data from the past. AI-centered models based on massive amounts of current economic data could fundamentally change that. By using very large high frequency datasets collected from online prices, consumer transactions, and job advertisements, central bank-designed AI models can “nowcast” and help provide an almost real-time picture of the economy. This is exactly what the Bank for International Settlements’ 2026 Project Spectrum is trying to accomplish using the European Central Bank’s Daily Price Dataset, which has billions of data points of daily prices for tens of millions of products. Hence, these models can detect shifts (minor and major) in the economy in real time, more effectively identify inflationary pressures sooner, and better distinguish data from noise.

Nowcasting becomes especially important in an increasingly geoeconomically charged global economic landscape, where tariffs and non-tariff trade barriers, geopolitical tensions, and disruptions in supply chains are rampant and more frequent and, hence, can lead to more volatility and unpredictability in economic outcomes.

And yet, forecasting is still an essential part of a central bank’s effective operations. This is because monetary policy impacts economic variables with lags, making it necessary for central bankers to forecast the direction of the economy in the future, not just understand where it is now.

Therefore, AI-heavy nowcasting should not replace forecasting. Both are needed, so central banks should try to come up with a new framework where both are used. After all, better understanding of how the economy is doing in real time can substantially help central bankers to make better forecasts of the economy’s direction in the future (“looking out the window,” to quote Warsh) and hence make their monetary policy more effective and accurate.

OCTOBER 16 | 3:33 AM ET

The Global South confronts a new dilemma 

Kerschyl Singh
Bretton Woods 2.0 fellow at the Atlantic Council’s GeoEconomics Center

On Friday morning, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s acknowledged that US monetary policy creates spillovers for the rest of the world, during his fireside chat with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. Two floors above them, shortly after the conversation wrapped, civil society leaders gathered to show what that spillover looks like in practice for the Global South.

The textbook “impossible trilemma” holds that an economic policymaker can choose only two of three policy goals: a fixed exchange rate, the free flow of capital, and independent monetary policy. The consensus among civil society leaders gathered for Friday’s panel on “Managing Financial Openness in the Global South” settled on a crucial argument: for many economies, the impossible trilemma has become a simple dilemma. An independent monetary policy is only possible if a country’s capital account is adaptively managed to mitigate domestic financial market frictions. The panelists discussed research covering more than fifty countries over twenty years, showing that capital controls are necessary to preserve monetary autonomy and ensure macro-financial stability.

Research by the economist Helene Rey showed that these countries have less autonomy than previously assumed. Domestic financial conditions—the exchange rate, inflation, interest rates—move closely with the global financial cycles. Those cycles are driven by global interest rates, which are primarily driven by the US Federal Reserve rate.

Warsh gave no hints in his conversation with Georgieva about what the Fed will do next on interest rates, while assuring the audience that domestic “price stability” was his number one goal. But what the Fed decides will have ramifications far outside the United States.

OCTOBER 16 | 1:13 AM ET

Bangkok has been relatively quiet on this far-reaching reform

Nicole Goldin
Nonresident senior fellow at the GeoEconomics Center; former lead economist at the World Bank and senior advisor to State Department and USAID

Ahead of the meetings, the IMF and World Bank released their Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries, the first overhaul since 2017. This tool for assessing debt risk is important because it shapes which countries are eligible for International Development Association grants and debt restructuring via the Common Framework. The problem is, it’s barely being talked about in Bangkok.

From a development perspective, the biggest change in the new reform is a new long-term module that extends projections and accounts for the impact on debt of spending on education, health, climate adaptation, and infrastructure necessary for growth.

The review’s simulations make the case. An increase in public spending of 1 percent of gross domestic product lifts long-run output by roughly 1.9 percent for health and education and about 3 percent for infrastructure.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva noted this week that low-income countries’ debt service costs surged from 6 percent to 14 percent of revenue in a decade, even as their overall debt has decreased.

Despite the fact that the framework influences restructurings and credit ratings (and ultimately the cost of capital), the creditors haven’t really talked about this new long-term module. The Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable’s progress report on Wednesday gave the new framework a single procedural bullet and said nothing of its long-term module.

At the same time, the debtors’ side hasn’t necessarily given it much attention either. The new UN-backed Borrowers’ Platform, which held its first Governing Council meeting here on Monday, warned that interest costs are crowding out health, education, and climate spending. But it made no mention of the framework that judges how much of that debt is sustainable.

The framework will start in late 2027. But the bigger question is whether the IMF will apply this framework when it designs its lending programs in response to Article IV country health checks.

The framework can now show that investing in people pays for itself on the right terms, but it cannot set those terms. And in a statement to ministers yesterday, the US Treasury warned the IMF away from lending that “veers into development-policy lending,” suggesting the politics may not match the model.

OCTOBER 15 | 10:22 AM ET

Can Asian economies make the good times last?

Martin Mühleisen
Nonresident senior fellow at the GeoEconomics Center; former IMF chief of staff and strategy director

Almost thirty years after the Asian financial crisis engulfed the region in economic turmoil, South Korea and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) economies have again become an important motor for the global economy. They are benefiting from a global super-cycle in AI investment, while a declining bilateral flow of goods between the US and China has increased trade flows through Asian economies more generally.

At the same time, the region is becoming more exposed to geopolitical developments. China is its largest production partner, a major source of capital and intermediate goods, and an important consumer market. On the other hand, the United States remains a critical export destination, technology provider, investor, and security partner. Neither relationship can substitute for the other, but deteriorating relations between the two superpowers could make it more difficult for the region to keep its current dynamic.

For South Korea, the AI boom has produced exceptional demand for semiconductors and helped offset the effects of higher energy prices. But as former Bank of Korea Governor Changyong Rhee noted during an Atlantic Council discussion this week in Bangkok, the gains are concentrated in a few companies and partly reflect US restrictions on China’s access to advanced semiconductor equipment. China’s eventual technological progress—or a relaxation of these restrictions—could weaken South Korea’s current advantage.

China’s economic role is also changing. South Korean companies have benefited for many years from supplying and investing in the “factory of Asia.” However, Beijing’s export-oriented economic model means that South Korean companies are now confronting Chinese companies at home and abroad.

ASEAN economies face a related dilemma. Owing mainly to Chinese investment and inexpensive inputs, they have become tightly integrated into global supply chains. Yet new investment does not automatically create domestic capabilities: Much of the underlying research and technology is still under foreign control.

Volatility

The region may also face increased financial volatility. Rhee described how rapid gains in semiconductor shares increased foreign investors’ exposure to the South Korean market. Their subsequent portfolio rebalancing generated equity sales and purchases of dollars, putting downward pressure on the won even as South Korea’s current-account surplus expanded.

This complicates the distinction between strong and weak external positions, and memories of the 1997 crisis can make them difficult to accept. Countries therefore may face a choice between allowing the exchange rate to absorb external shocks and limiting its volatility, which could put unwanted constraints on monetary policy.

The region’s dependency on oil imports also means that higher prices could weaken trade balances and raise inflation, while shifts in the global risk appetite could generate capital outflows and exchange-rate pressures. Currency depreciation could complicate trade relations with the United States, and central banks would have a harder job weighing their price stability objective against the impact of policy decisions on the domestic economy.

Opportunity

To improve the foundations for stable economic growth, former Indonesian Finance Minister Chatib Basri at an Atlantic Council event this week called for domestic industry to collaborate with external partners across geopolitical camps. He pointed to a recent partnership between the Ford Motor Company, China’s Huayou Cobalt, and Vale Indonesia that could help Indonesia upgrade its nickel processing capabilities.

Sutapa Amornvivat, a Thai leader in digital integration, suggested that the digital economy offered another route to stronger economic growth. ASEAN’s Digital Economy Framework Agreement, due to be signed in November, could have a catalytic impact as it promotes digital payments and e-commerce more broadly.

First, however, ASEAN countries must decide how to combine competing technologies, data rules, security standards, and AI systems without dividing the regional market. They also would have to manage wide differences in digital infrastructure, energy availability, and skills across member states. Growing integration would indeed help the region to prepare for a turn in the economic cycle. Deepening trade under the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, moving toward interoperable payment systems, and improving energy networks could give East and Southeast Asian firms access to a market large enough to support innovation and real economies of scale, helping them to consolidate their gains if and when the economic cycle turns again.

OCTOBER 15 | 7:13 AM ET

Eurogroup President Kyriakos Pierrakakis on European resilience and reform

OCTOBER 15 | 6:10 AM ET

The new geoeconomics of inflation

Amin Mohseni-Cheraghlou
Macroeconomist with the GeoEconomics Center; former senior advisor to the executive director at the IMF and research economist at the World Bank

These days, central banks are asked to solve an inflation problem they did not create and cannot solve alone. From my observations here at the annual meetings, central bankers are not particularly happy about this. In any conversation in hallways and meeting rooms about inflation’s resurgence, supply-side factors are immediately mentioned—particularly by the monetary policy crowd.

The numbers tell the story. The IMF projects global headline inflation to rise from 4.1 percent in 2025 to 4.7 percent in 2026, with euro area inflation increasing from 2.1 to 3.1 percent and the US increasing from 2.7 to 3.6 percent.

This is partly driven by four factors that have nothing to do with monetary policy:

Persistent fiscal deficits increase aggregate demand.

Tariffs raise import costs, disrupt supply chains, and weaken competition, while industrial subsidies and efforts to reshore strategic production can further increase fiscal deficits and create supply bottlenecks.  

Conflicts and energy disruptions push up commodity prices, production costs, and defense spending (fueling those fiscal deficits).

Though largely forgotten in this year’s annual meetings, the increasing frequency and severity of climate-related extreme events cause spikes in government spending in response to crises, food prices (because of more floods and droughts), energy demand (for more cooling and heating), and insurance and risk premiums.  

To fight back, central banks have essentially one weapon in their arsenal: interest rates. So they can only confront inflationary pressures by suppressing aggregate demand through higher interest rates. They cannot reduce tariffs, resolve conflicts, expand energy supplies, reverse subsidies, or reduce defense expenditures.

In today’s geoeconomically charged landscape, price stability can no longer be treated as the exclusive responsibility of central banks. While central banks’ independence and their leadership in the fight against inflation are essential, confronting inflation requires greater coordination across monetary, fiscal, trade, industrial, and foreign policies. Otherwise, governments risk fueling inflation with one set of policies while forcing central banks to fight it at the expense of investment, employment, and growth.

OCTOBER 14 | 11:55 PM ET

To make the leap, Thailand needs to convert foreign investment into local capabilities

Amin Mohseni-Cheraghlou
Macroeconomist with the GeoEconomics Center; former senior advisor to the executive director at the IMF and research economist at the World Bank

It is rare to have four economists agree on one policy priority for a country’s growth prospects. My conversation yesterday with Santitarn Sathirathai (vice minister of finance for Thailand), Stephen Ndegwa (World Bank division director for Thailand and Myanmar), and Arnaud Dupoizat (the International Finance Corporation’s regional director for East Asia) was one of those rare occasions. When asked about one policy that tops their list of priorities in the next three to five years to help Thailand’s ambition in achieving high-income status by 2037, all three mentioned increasing productivity and domestic value added in the Thai economy—exactly my main finding a few weeks ago when I wrote “the measure of success should not be the amount of investment Thailand attracts, but the value it creates at home.”

This is true, not only for Thailand but also for all ASEAN economies. The amounts of foreign trade relative to the size of these economies are some of the highest in the world. Foreign direct investment (FDI) has been fueling their industrial base, especially in the past decade because of “China + One” policies pursued by multinational companies. However, the share of domestic value added in ASEAN economies (especially the bigger economies known as the ASEAN-5: Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Singapore) has been shrinking, productivity has more or less stalled, and high-paying jobs have been scarce.

So, while more FDI is always welcomed, turning “that FDI into local capabilities, better [small and medium-sized enterprises], better skills, and better jobs,” as Santitarn put it, is what is most needed for Thailand and other ASEAN-5 economies, for them to continue growing and avoid the middle-income trap.

OCTOBER 14 | 11:33 PM ET

The global economic safety cushions are wearing thin

Kerschyl Singh
Bretton Woods 2.0 fellow at the Atlantic Council’s GeoEconomics Center

While the IMF’s World Economic Outlook lays out resilient growth and inflation forecasts, the Global Financial Stability Report makes the detailed case around the risks and vulnerabilities in the outlook. Three themes are worth mentioning, and the key vulnerability is that all three have meaningful interaction with the bond market. 

First, the technology sector’s AI investments take up a huge part of the debt market, with a 10 percent share of global investment-grade corporate bonds (vs. 1 percent in 2024). Second, hedge funds held about 9 percent of US government bonds in 2025, more than double their 2022 share. Third, the energy shock beginning in late February shook global markets.

It means governments are paying more to borrow. The interest rate on ten-year government bonds has increased about 1.5 percentage points in France, 1.25 points in the United States, and emerging economies outside China pay about 0.65 more (see chart below). While higher bond yields increase debt interest payments for governments, they also reduce the regulatory required capital value of bonds held by banks and hedge funds.

IMF reports make an important point that none of these risks in isolation is a crisis. However, the combination of risks shows a far more elevated chance of a crisis, with thinning safety cushions. Instead of governments taking steps to lower debt, they are spending to shield consumers and businesses from the energy shock. 

To understand this complex scenario, the Global Financial Stability Report developed a stress test for banks against an AI crash, an energy shock, and higher interest rates. The test found that 22 percent of global banking assets fell below its 7 percent capital safety line. Last year’s test found 18 percent of banking assets falling below the safety line, implying that the interaction of risks is eroding resilience.

The weakness, the IMF found, lies with banks that lend heavily to non-banks, such as private credit and private equity funds. Policymakers should act while they still have time to curb risky borrowing. One way the IMF advises is to stretch out government debt maturity so less comes due at once. The IMF adds that governments should rebuild fiscal space “in a way not to complicate the task of monetary policy,” and in a way that strengthens institutions. 

OCTOBER 14 | 10:35 PM ET

UN under-secretary-general: Nepal is feeling”compounding effects” of the climate and supply-chain crises

Jorge Moreira da Silva, United Nations under-secretary-general and executive director of the United Nations Office for Project Services, joins the Atlantic Council’s Michael Kugelman ahead of a trip to Nepal to discuss how the country is dealing with devastating floods and the fallout from the Strait of Hormuz crisis.

OCTOBER 14 | 9:18 PM ET

At a high-stakes meeting today, the G20 is searching for balance

Josh Lipsky
Chair of international economics at the Atlantic Council; former IMF adviser

The Group of Twenty (G20) finance ministers and central bank governors meet Thursday in Bangkok, their last chance to all sit down together before the end of the US G20 presidency and the leaders’ summit in December in Miami. Their to-do list is not short. When they met in Asheville, North Carolina, over the summer, they agreed to focus on tackling macroeconomic imbalances (by which the US means China’s dangerous trillion-dollar trade surplus), bringing down energy prices by restoring transit in the Strait of Hormuz, dealing with sovereign debt, and coordinating across borders on regulation of digital assets. 

So they could be forgiven for not having made too much progress on some of the world’s thorniest economic challenges in the past six weeks. Like any group project nearing a deadline, this meeting becomes about what they actually want to prioritize with the little time left in the US presidency of the G20. The problem is that the person who would chair the meeting, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, has decided to skip the trip to Bangkok. That means leadership will fall to his colleagues, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh (who is attending his first IMF-World Bank meetings as Fed chair) and Bessent’s deputy, Francis Brooke. The rest of the G20 countries have, despite major differences with the US, largely supported a wide swath of the agenda—perhaps most importantly on imbalances. Notable exceptions include, unsurprisingly, China and Russia. 

All eyes will soon turn toward the UK as the next host, and already I’ve heard conversations this week about what the UK will and won’t take forward from this year. 

The G20 has shown its worth time and again when crisis strikes and you need the world’s financial leaders to all coordinate quickly. Given some of the stark warnings about AI, debt, and energy risks this week in Bangkok, it would be good if the group finishes this year strong and heads into 2027 with momentum. That makes today’s meeting one of its more important in recent memory.

OCTOBER 14 | 7:30 AM ET

The jobs are coming. Will the money follow?

Nicole Goldin
Nonresident senior fellow at the GeoEconomics Center; former lead economist at the World Bank and senior advisor to State Department and USAID

Last month, the World Bank announced with much fanfare that it had attracted $112 billion in private capital to augment its own spending to create jobs and drive development in emerging economies, more than triple the level from four years ago.

Yet serious questions remain about allocation, absorption, and whether countries can receive financing at the scale required to generate enough jobs to fill the projected global job shortage of 800 million for new workforce entrants over the next decade. Today’s hot-ticket session discussing investment opportunities in emerging markets—the third leg of the World Bank’s “triple crown” of flagship events at these meetings—was encouraging, but it didn’t necessarily render answers.

At every turn at the mic so far this week, World Bank President Ajay Banga has leaned hard into the jobs agenda he oriented the Bank around, as seen this morning as well as in the other two legs of the triple crown: Monday’s session on “small AI” and Tuesday’s on finance for small businesses.

Announced Tuesday, the Bank’s new strategy for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises—which employ some 90 percent of workers in developing economies—aims to deliver technological advancements such as digital payments, e‑invoicing, and cash‑flow data. These tools could transform how lenders assess risk and unlock finance (and thus growth) for millions of small firms that generate millions of jobs.

Similarly, task‑specific small‑AI tools that require less compute, energy, data, and infrastructure are creating opportunities in sectors such as health and agriculture. Yet risks persist: AI may exacerbate skills mismatches and create a K‑shaped labor market, where high‑skill workers capture gains while low‑skill workers fall further behind.

Across all these areas, trust, security, scale, and inequality threaten traction—alongside the broader geoeconomic headwinds of fragmentation, declining investment, and rising debt that also demand (and are seemingly gaining) attention and action this week.

There is emerging evidence and momentum around many of the ideas in the jobs agenda. Before we wrap up on Saturday, I’ll be watching to see whether the necessary political will, financing, and multilateral coordination will follow.

OCTOBER 14 | 6:48 AM ET

ECB President Christine Lagarde on European payment sovereignty, AI, and inflation

OCTOBER 14 | 4:09 AM ET

The sun is no longer shining, and urgency is rising to tackle soaring debt at last

Bart Piasecki
Associate director at the GeoEconomics Center

The IMF has been warning policymakers about the growing need for fiscal adjustment for a while. In 2017, then IMF Managing Director Christine Lagarde famously spoke about “fixing the roof while the sun is shining.” Since then, the message of the IMF’s Fiscal Monitor has been consistent: Deficits are too high and can’t be supported by current levels of growth. Public spending should be more efficient and support measures better targeted. Revenue administrations need to be strengthened and tax collection broadened and streamlined. Yet countries around the world continued running large deficits.

They could afford to do so because of the favorable environment. Decades of low interest rates offset by relatively decent growth allowed governments to carry large deficits and manage rising debt fairly easily.

But that’s not the case anymore. Inflation has been running high in major economies such as the US and the eurozone for more than five years. And recent inflationary pressures stemming from the energy price shock are forcing monetary authorities to act. Interest rate hikes in major economies are pushing bond yields higher, further pushing borrowing costs up. Markets are signaling that this trajectory cannot continue, with bond yields rising to two-decade highs across the board.

With a debt pile as large as it was after World War II, sticky inflation, and high interest rates, there is a sense of urgency to get serious. That’s the message IMF Director of Fiscal Affairs Rodrigo Valdés was pushing when we spoke this morning in our studios in Bangkok, as Valdés presented the newest version of the Fiscal Monitor. The fiscal outlook is grim, but this is exactly the role of the IMF—to help policymakers here in Bangkok, but also at home, to design the policy mix that helps them navigate through this.

OCTOBER 14 | 3:22 AM ET

World Bank’s Lisandro Martín: “What we need to do is complement public financing with private financing”

Lisandro Martín, the director of the Outcomes Department in the Senior Managing Director’s Office at the World Bank Group, joined the GeoEconomic Center’s Juliet Lancey to discuss how the World Bank is responding to the decline in government investment in global development.

OCTOBER 14 | 1:28 AM ET

The case for taxing better, not taxing more

Hung Tran
Nonresident senior fellow at the GeoEconomics Center, senior fellow at the Policy Center for the New South, former deputy director at the IMF

The IMF has just released its October 2026 Fiscal Monitor, with its clear and simple advice encapsulated in the title of the document: “Taxing better to boost growth.” Elevated levels of public debt and debt servicing due to high interest rates have put pressure on authorities to mobilize fiscal resources for development, social, and, increasingly, defense needs. However, public resistance to higher rates of taxation has strengthened, practically everywhere.

Against that backdrop, the Fiscal Monitor has sensibly focused on two pieces of practical advice: improving the design of taxation—in particular the value-added tax—to avoid distortions and disincentives to production; and improving tax collection procedures. These reforms can raise revenue while lowering production costs and easing compliance burdens, encouraging investment and business growth, and improving incentives to work and innovate—without worsening inequality.

The Fiscal Monitor highlights that the potential gains from efficient taxation are sizable. Specifically, reducing value-added tax–related production and consumption distortion could produce welfare gains of up to 0.8 percent of GDP in emerging market and developing countries. For example, the IMF speaks of a “clear and present danger” in commodity and global bond markets, based on the plausible scenario where it takes until the end of 2027 to see the full recovery of oil shipments and long-term yields increase because central banks are slow to respond to inflationary pressures. What could possibly go wrong by postponing fiscal belt-tightening for just another year?

Finance leaders are finally grasping their geopolitics problem

Josh Lipsky
Chair of international economics at the Atlantic Council; former IMF adviser

Today the world’s financial leaders opened the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank facing a more daunting geopolitical landscape than at any time since perhaps the 1961 meetings in Vienna, which took place thirty-six days after construction of the Berlin Wall began.

Ministers from 191 countries are meeting to discuss and debate the need for cooperation on everything from AI guardrails to the risk of a sovereign debt crisis in France. Few expect any concrete breakthroughs. But as our team assembles in Thailand, I am more optimistic than I have been in a decade of taking part in these gatherings.

That’s because I am finally seeing signs that financial leaders understand that they cannot divorce their policymaking from geopolitics.

Three years ago, when the Hamas terrorist attack on Israel occurred on the eve of the annual meetings, the ministers and central bank governors didn’t want to deal with the potential financial fallout. Now, many of the governments actually want to start tackling the most complex international problems, from the impact of sanctions on the dollar to China’s economic imbalances. And all of these leaders now talk about how to adapt to a world that is being reshaped, instead of pretending as if we are going back to the old system of unfettered globalization.

The major news items heading into this week’s meetings included the US committing to buy Russian diesel and the Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport. And country delegations are telling me they want to address these issues head on, not dodge the questions.

This is not to say that the delegates have all—or any—of the answers. But the first step in solving any problem is recognizing there is one. After years of ignoring the geopolitical realities staring them in the face, the world’s financial policymakers are finally showing they are ready to do what their predecessors who created these institutions did—link prosperity with security.

How advanced economies’ surging debt is impacting emerging markets

Amin Mohseni-Cheraghlou
Macroeconomist with the GeoEconomics Center; former senior advisor to the executive director at the IMF and research economist at the World Bank

Combined sovereign debt in advanced economies has now reached nearly 110 percent of GDP, including 126 percent of GDP in the United States. These debt levels, coupled with persistently high interest rates, have knock-on effects for developing countries and emerging markets (EMDEs).

First, as advanced economies borrow more, they push up global borrowing costs. Higher US Treasury yields—a global benchmark—make it more expensive for EMDEs to access international capital markets, even when their economic fundamentals remain sound.

Second, higher returns on advanced economies’ assets (which are deemed safer) will induce a capital withdrawal from EMDEs into advanced economies. These outflows put downward pressure on local currencies of EMDEs, making imports more expensive and fueling inflation. These dynamics will force central banks to increase domestic interest rates to stabilize currencies and contain inflation, weakening private investment, domestic job creation, and economic growth.

Third, higher global interest rates intensify already heavy debt burdens in EMDEs. According to the World Bank, developing countries paid a record $415 billion in external debt interest in 2024. Moreover, between 2022 and 2024, they paid $741 billion more in external debt service than they received in new financing, the largest gap in the past fifty years. Rising debt-servicing costs leave EMDEs with fewer resources to invest in infrastructure, education, healthcare, and other development priorities, undermining their long-term development and growth prospects.

Finally, mounting fiscal pressures in advanced economies can weaken demand for imports from EMDEs. Through these channels—higher borrowing costs, tighter financing conditions, currency depreciation, higher inflation, shrinking fiscal space, and reduced exports—EMDEs are increasingly bearing the consequences of fiscal and monetary decisions made in advanced economies, over which they have no control. The bottom line: Advanced economies are accumulating the debt, but EMDEs are increasingly paying the price.

The IMF just reviewed some of its key policies. What will change?

Martin Mühleisen
Nonresident senior fellow at the GeoEconomics Center; former IMF chief of staff and strategy director

Four major reviews published in recent days offer a candid account of the IMF’s core work. They cover debt sustainability in low-income countries, program design and conditionality, the financial sector assessment program (FSAP), and economic surveillance. Taken together, the reports call for more realistic analysis, greater selectivity, better integration across policy areas, and stronger follow-through. Here’s a quick rundown:

In the past, the low-income debt sustainability framework has concentrated on external debt in foreign currency. Domestic borrowing in local currency has grown in importance, however, opening up new avenues for shocks and risk transmission. The review proposes new indicators for gross financing needs and interest payments, a domestic-debt module, and a stress test for domestic financing. This matters because an incomplete diagnosis can delay debt restructuring, encourage additional lending into an unsustainable situation, and eventually impose larger costs on citizens and creditors alike.

The review of IMF program conditionality calls for more credible assumptions underlying programs’ macroeconomic frameworks, stronger contingency planning, and better sequencing of structural reforms. For the latter, it suggests that programs develop a medium-term reform strategy centered on measures critical for program success. This is an implicit acknowledgment that programs can become overloaded: Excess conditionality can consume scarce administrative capacity and distract from the reforms on which recovery actually depends.

The surveillance review seeks sharper prioritization for the IMF’s country work, clearer tests of macroeconomic relevance for topics that are being covered, stronger macrofinancial analysis, and more contingent policy advice. At the same time, it also asks staff to deepen work on external spillovers, AI, structural policies, and emerging risks. These are legitimate subjects but, without clear prioritization, Article IV consultations may fail to convey the fund’s most consequential advice. Indeed, the question of how the IMF should communicate its advice was not a subject of the review, an important shortcoming that hampers the traction of IMF policy advice.

The FSAP review responds to an increasingly complex global financial system by proposing more modular and risk-based assessments, closer integration with Article IV consultations, and more prioritized, actionable recommendations. Indeed, the program’s remit now extends well beyond its initial bank focus to include nonbank institutions, digital finance, cyber threats, climate risks, and cross-border interconnections. Again, the risk is dilution of resources and weak follow-up that can leave material vulnerabilities unresolved between assessments.

These are sound recommendations, but they are also familiar from earlier reviews. This creates grounds for skepticism about whether IMF management and the Executive Board will heed their own advice this time.

The ultimate test for the IMF to operate differently will arise in everyday program decisions, especially in cases involving large exposures and surveillance outcomes of shareholders that pose risks for the global economy. Those are precisely the cases where politically influenced judgments can carry the greatest costs.

To assess whether these recommendations gain traction, the IMF could publish an annual implementation scorecard. For major deviations, the institution should explain the reasons for departing from the new guidance. This would preserve the discretion required for country work while making review outcomes more transparent. Review departments would remain responsible for consistency, and management and the Executive Board would be placed on the record for the institutional choices that follow.

Without such visible accountability, the next review cycle five years from now is likely to return to many of the same questions about realism, selectivity, integration, and follow-through. By then, the IMF may again look back on program failures or surveillance misses that could have been avoided by applying the lessons so convincingly presented by its own staff over the past few weeks.

The world economy is undergoing three concurrent shocks—the energy supply shock, the AI demand shock, and the public sector debt shock. They interact to push up long-term interest rates—which could pose economic and financial risks.

Conflict in the Middle East has disrupted the supply of oil and gas—raising crude oil prices to more than one hundred dollars a barrel, which is fueling median one-year median global inflation expectations to 3.9 percent, the highest since May 2023. Goldman Sachs has estimated that global AI investment expenditure would exceed one trillion dollars in 2026—or 0.9 percent of global GDP. This is projected to rise to 1.3 percent in 2027 and 1.4 percent in 2028, boosting global GDP growth by between 0.5 percent and 1.5 percent in the period ahead. 

At the same time, public debt of advanced economies has reached a new high of $102 trillion or 91 percent of global GDP. Driving the rising public debt level in advanced economies has been persistently high fiscal deficits of 5 to 6 percent of global GDP, generating substantial interest payments.

The three shocks mentioned above appear to impact the three key components making up long-term nominal interest rates. The AI funding need has triggered a rise in the equilibrium real interest rate r*, estimated to be 2.95 percent as measured by the Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) yields. The energy supply shock has driven the inflation premium—the price investors demand to compensate for the risk of inflation increases—estimated at 2.36 percent. These make up the ten-year nominal Treasury yield at 5.31 percent as of October 5. The term premium—to compensate investors for holding long maturity securities—which is embedded in the real rates and inflation premium, has been estimated at 1.08 percent.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva noted in her curtain-raiser speech for the meetings that high rates are likely to remain over the long term, with negative implications for economic growth prospects and equity valuation. Stocks in the S&P 500 index are richly valued at around 26.6 in price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios—well above the long-term average of 16.2. More concerning is the fact that the ten-year Shiller CAPE (Cyclically Adjusted P/E) ratio has exceeded 41, about 2.3 standard deviations above the modern-age average—putting stocks in strongly overvalued territory. Moreover, there exists an extreme concentration risk in AI and high-tech sectors—with ten top companies approaching 40 percent of the S&P 500 index. This could give any market correction a wider systemic spillover impact than otherwise would be the case.

Economic growth drivers have also been concentrated in the AI/high-tech sector, whose capital expenditures account for 1.8 to 2.5 percent of US GDP, but has contributed about half of US GDP growth in recent quarters.

In short, persistently high interest rates, driven by a variety of factors, pose a threat to currently overvalued US equity markets burdened by extreme concentration risk; the materialization of these risks would negatively impact economic growth prospects. Policymakers can ameliorate this challenging situation by putting their fiscal houses in order—reducing budget deficits to relieve some pressure on interest rates and hoping that all the AI investment will soon produce productivity improvement and stronger growth, which could make the economy and financial markets more resilient to high rates and equity valuations.

The new geoeconomics of Bretton Woods

When government officials, investors, policymakers, and academics gather in Bangkok on October 12 for the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings, they will confront a global economy markedly changed since their 2023 meeting in Marrakesh. Heightened by geoeconomic competition, protectionism, tariffs, and economic and military conflict, the global trade, investment, and supply chain maps are being redrawn, and a new global order is in the making. Against this backdrop of increasing global fragmentation, the main challenge facing the Bretton Woods Institutions is preserving international economic cooperation and coordination as the issues facing member economies and their populations become ever more global and transnational in scope.

Trade, investment, technology, finance, energy, and critical minerals are increasingly intertwined with national security. The United States, China, the European Union, and a growing number of middle powers are using tariffs, subsidies, export controls, investment restrictions, industrial policy, and supply-chain strategies to protect domestic industries and secure strategic advantage. Production networks are being reorganized around resilience and political alignment, while global imbalances are widening. At the same time, developing countries are facing extraordinary pressure from conflict, high debt, fiscal strain, climate risks, demographic change, and rapid technological transformation (namely AI and data centers). Globalization is not ending—it is becoming more contested and fragmented.

This shift presents a fundamental challenge for the IMF and World Bank. Both institutions were established on the belief that international economic integration, backed by major powers, could generate shared benefits when accompanied by macroeconomic stability, development finance, and international rules.
